insights.title: Peanut butter banana “power” overnight oats
insights.summary: Five minutes tonight, a protein-packed breakfast tomorrow.
body: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] Prep time: 5 minutes. Makes 1 serving. Enjoy it cold straight from the fridge, or warm it in the microwave for about 45 seconds if you’d like something warm during a chilly night feed.
Ingredients
• 1/2 cup rolled (old-fashioned) oats, for fiber and steady energy
• 1/2 cup milk of your choice: dairy, soy, almond or oat
• 1/4 cup plain or vanilla Greek yogurt, for a creamy texture and protein to keep you full longer
• 1 tbsp chia seeds or ground flaxseed, for fiber and omega-3 fats
• 1 tbsp peanut butter (or almond butter), for healthy fats and extra protein
• 1 tsp maple syrup or honey (optional), for a touch of sweetness
• 1/2 tsp cinnamon and a splash of vanilla extract
• 1/2 ripe banana, mashed or sliced (mashed blends into the oats; sliced adds texture on top)
How to make it
1. Layer the jar: add the oats, chia seeds (or flaxseed) and cinnamon to a clean mason jar or airtight container.
2. Add the wet ingredients: pour in the milk, Greek yogurt, vanilla and maple syrup (if using). Stir well so there are no dry pockets of seeds or oats.
3. Stir in the good stuff: add the peanut butter and mashed banana (or save the banana slices for the morning).
4. Rest and set: close the lid and refrigerate for at least 4 hours, or ideally overnight.
5. Wake up and eat: give it a good stir. If it’s too thick, add a splash more milk. Top with banana slices or an extra drizzle of peanut butter.

Tip for busy moms: make three or four jars at once on a Sunday, or while your partner is on baby duty. They keep in the fridge for up to 4 days, so a nourishing breakfast is ready the second hunger strikes.
Honey is fine for you, but never give honey to a baby under 12 months.

insights.title: The thirst trap: keep a drink within reach
body: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] If you’ve spent more than five minutes with a newborn, you’ve probably felt it: the nursing thirst. One moment you’re leaning back in your glider, settling in for a feed, and the next your throat feels like sandpaper. That’s exactly when you realize your water bottle is on the kitchen counter, fifteen feet and one sleeping baby away.
Consider this your official postpartum reminder: never sit down to feed your baby without a drink within arm’s reach.
Why thirst hits so hard
• Feeding hormones: many moms feel a sudden, strong thirst as soon as they start nursing or pumping. It’s your body’s cue to drink while it makes milk.
• Recovery and broken sleep: healing from birth, short nights and night sweats all add up. Not drinking enough can show up as brain fog, tiredness or headaches.
You don’t need to force down extra water. The CDC’s advice is simple: drink when you’re thirsty, and keep a drink handy so you can.
How to set up your drink station
1. Go one-handed: skip screw-top bottles. Choose an insulated tumbler with a built-in straw or a flip-top lid you can open with one hand while holding a squirmy baby.
2. Go big: a 30 to 40 oz (about 0.9 to 1.2 liter) tumbler keeps ice water cold for hours, so you won’t need to get up for a refill mid-feed.

3. Mix it up: water is king, but variety helps at 3 a.m. Try electrolyte packets in water if you like them, coconut water, or a cup of decaf tea once it has cooled to warm. Keep hot drinks away from your baby, and check with your provider before using herbal teas while breastfeeding, since some aren’t recommended.
The rule of threes

One bottle isn’t enough: bottles get lost, knocked over or left in another room. Aim for three: one by your feeding chair, one by your bed for night wake-ups, and one in the diaper bag for when you’re out.
When you’re busy growing and feeding a tiny human, taking care of yourself can start with something as simple as a glass of water. What’s your go-to water bottle?

insights.title: Rest counts, too
insights.summary: Lying down for ten minutes is enough.
body: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] You don't need to fill every quiet moment. If the baby is settled and someone is around, it's okay to put your feet up, even for a few minutes.

insights.title: Choking: be prepared
insights.summary: Know what to do before you need it.
body: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] The Choking and gagging guide shows which foods to avoid or change at each age, and how to tell gagging from choking. A baby first-aid and CPR course is a good way to feel prepared.
If your baby is choking and cannot breathe, cry or make a sound, call 911 right away.
